title: Share Bench
description: Deal a heap onto plates one round at a time, name the four numbers, and try one plate, as many plates as things, and no plates at all.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded card holding the running count, the working area, the question, the answer box and the keypad; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it, the phase dots and the phase and question counts at the right.

writeup.why: Share a heap equally onto plates, name the four numbers that come out of it, and find out which sharings cannot be done at all.
writeup.look: A tray of counters at the left, a row of plates along the middle with a leftover dish beside them, and four name tags waiting at the side.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Share Bench' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the rounds dealt against the counters the heap began with, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each round lands on the plates, which makes it one plate's share, and the second fixed at the size of the heap. On the first phase it carries the rows and the counters in a row instead. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The tray occupies 320 by 300 at 64,220, its counters in deep blue laid in rows of ten, at most ninety-nine of them, none overlapping. The plate dial sits under it, 320 by 56 at 64,532, running from none upwards, and the four name tags lie below that, each 150 by 44, at 64,604, 234,604, 64,660 and 234,660, reading dividend, divisor, quotient and remainder. The fact card runs across the top of the bench, 660 by 110 at 420,210, holding the same counters as equal rows with the multiplication written under them; turning it swings the rows round a quarter turn so that rows become columns, and writes one division for each reading. The plate rail stands under the card, 520 by 280 at 420,334, laying out whatever number of plates the dial sets in rows of ten, in amber, every plate on one deal the same size and none overlapping, so twelve plates stand in two rows and thirty-four in four. Deal a round lifts exactly as many counters out of the tray as there are plates and puts one on each at the same moment, and one plate's share is printed under each plate in green as it settles. The leftover dish stands apart from the plates, 150 by 130 at 956,334, taking in vermilion what cannot go round; its lid stays open while it holds as many counters as there are plates, and then every plate that could take one more lights. The rule bay sits under the dish, 150 by 150 at 956,478, four keys reading one plate, as many plates as counters, an empty tray and no plates at all. With no plates the deal control stays unlit and the caption says there is nowhere to put a share; no number is drawn anywhere on the stage for it. The check bar runs along the foot, 686 by 70 at 420,640, and multiplies the plates by one plate's share, adds the dish, and builds the heap again in rows of ten beside the tray. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a count is asked for. On the second phase a word pad sits over it with the four names, dividend, divisor, quotient and remainder, and on the fourth it carries a key reading not possible, so a division by zero is answered by press and never with a number. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the dividend, the whole being shared and any total, is deep blue; the divisor, and the plates, groups or envelopes it makes, is amber; the quotient and each equal share are green; what is left over, at one step or at the end, is vermilion; a multiple of the divisor, tried on a ladder or taken away as a chunk, is rose; and a zero written in the quotient because the number was smaller than the divisor is grey. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because what is left over is told by the dish or the slot it sits in, a quotient digit by the row it sits in, and a multiple by the rung or the column that holds it, before any of them is told by a colour, and every rule, bracket, cell edge and guide line is near-black. Grey never means faint: a zero in the quotient is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. The leftover dish is never inside a plate and never under one. It stands apart at full strength, and it keeps its lid open until what it holds is smaller than the number of plates, because a leftover that could still go round is not a remainder yet.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last heap the child shared, its plates and leftover dish still drawn, with the four name tags where the child dropped them and the check written underneath.

phases.win: both division facts settle under the fact card, one for each number that was multiplied
phases.does: reads the rows one way and writes a division, then turns the card and writes the other
phases.goal: a multiplication fact with no zero in it gives two division facts, one for each number that was multiplied
phases.says: Read the rows one way. Now turn the card. What does each way divide by?
phases.check: Away from the screen: lay out four rows of six counters, then write both divisions they show.
phases.feels: one set of rows, read from two sides, and each side divides by a different number
phases.hands: Lay out counters in four rows of six on a desk. Read them as four rows of six, then walk round to the other side of the desk and read the same counters as six rows of four. Write one division from each side, and ask what number each one divided by. Then take six away from the whole heap again and again, counting the takes, and ask which of the two divisions the number of takes matches.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what is the product on the card? Second rung, the phase's: how many are in each row, and how many rows are there? Third rung: the card is cut to two rows of three and the child writes both divisions from it before the larger card comes back. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the recap's worked model turns six fifteens into ninety divided by fifteen and nothing else, so a single division looks like the whole of the job.
wrong.move: writes one division from the fact and stops, as though a multiplication could be undone only one way.
wrong.screen: the fact card turns round on its own with the counters left exactly where they stand, and the rows are read the other way, thirteen rows of nine where there were nine rows of thirteen. A second blank division line opens under the child's first one, which stays written, and the new rows light one at a time while their count climbs at the top left.

wrong.why: twelve is the number written again and again down the working, so it is the number the eye keeps meeting, and the question's how many times is easy to hear as how many.
wrong.move: answers twelve when asked how many times twelve could be taken away from eighty-four.
wrong.screen: the takes are replayed from the tray one at a time, each take of twelve lifting off as one group and landing in a row along the bench, and the running count climbs by one for each take, not by twelve, until the tray is empty at seven. The child's twelve stays in the slot and the row of seven takes lies beside it, counted.

phases.screen: counters laid out in equal rows, with a fact card reading the multiplication above them
phases.soWhat: A multiplication fact with no zero in it gives two division facts, one for each number that was multiplied.

phases.win: the four tags settle on the heap, the plate dial, one plate's share and the dish
phases.does: deals the heap a round at a time, then drops each name tag on the thing it names
phases.goal: the dividend is shared by the divisor, the quotient is each share and the remainder is what is left
phases.says: Deal one to every plate each round. Which number is being shared?
phases.check: Sixty-five seeds go equally into four pots. Point to each of the four numbers, and say what each one means.
phases.feels: four names, four different things on the bench, and each tag has only one place to land
phases.hands: Count out sixty-five counters and set out four paper plates. Deal one counter onto each plate a round at a time, saying the round aloud. When too few are left to go round, move them into a saucer. Then write four cards reading dividend, divisor, quotient and remainder, and lay each card on the thing it names.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which number is being shared? Second rung, the phase's: into how many parts? Third rung: the bench is cut to a heap of nine on two plates, and the child tags all four numbers before the larger heap comes back. The word pad stays open.

wrong.why: a division has a bigger number and a smaller one, and the answer to a sharing has always sounded like the small end of it.
wrong.move: calls six the quotient in seventy-nine shared among six, because it is the smaller of the two numbers in the story.
wrong.screen: the quotient tag is left lying where the child dropped it, on the plate dial, and the bench deals the seventy-nine a round at a time onto six plates: the round count at the top left climbs to thirteen and one plate's share reads thirteen underneath it. The words quotient and divisor are lit side by side on the tag rail, and one plate is lit with its count.

wrong.why: a counter on its own looks as if it belongs to somebody, and the plates are the only places on the bench that hold counters for anyone.
wrong.move: drops the remainder tag on one of the plates, because the leftover counter looks like one more share.
wrong.screen: the leftover counter is carried to that plate, which now holds fourteen while the other five hold thirteen, and the six plates are drawn plainly unequal side by side. The empty dish beside them lights, the counter walks back into it, and the plates settle level again with the child's tag still lying where it fell.

phases.screen: a heap in the tray, a row of plates, an empty leftover dish and four name tags at the side
phases.soWhat: The dividend is shared by the divisor, the quotient is each share, and the remainder is what is left.

phases.win: one more round leaves fewer in the dish than there are plates, and the check bar rebuilds the heap exactly
phases.does: tries to close the dish, deals one more round instead, then runs the check bar
phases.goal: the remainder is always smaller than the divisor, and divisor times quotient add remainder gives the dividend
phases.says: Look at the dish. Could every plate still take one more?
phases.check: Someone divides by five and says six are left over. Tell them what is wrong without working out the division.
phases.feels: a leftover as big as the plates is not a leftover yet, it is one more round waiting
phases.hands: Share fifty-eight counters among seven plates, but stop on purpose after seven rounds with nine still in the saucer. Ask whether the saucer could give every plate one more. Deal the extra round, count what is left, and then build the heap again: seven plates of eight, and add the two in the saucer.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many counters are in the dish? Second rung, the phase's: how many plates are there? Third rung: the bench is cut to eleven counters on three plates with the deal stopped after two rounds, and the child decides whether to deal again. Nothing already dealt is cleared.

wrong.why: the dealing has to stop somewhere, and a pile that is left looks like a leftover whatever its size.
wrong.move: stops dealing and writes the nine in the dish as the remainder, though seven of them could still go round.
wrong.screen: the dish lid stays open and all seven plates light, with seven of the nine counters in the dish lit to match them. The deal control lights, and one more round is dealt from the dish: each plate takes one, the dish is left holding two, and the lid closes by itself. The child's nine stays in the slot beside the new count, nothing marked.

wrong.why: the multiplication is the part that feels like the check, and the dish looks like something left out of the sum on purpose.
wrong.move: checks by multiplying the plates by the share and stops, without adding what is in the dish.
wrong.screen: the check bar builds the heap from the plates alone, seven rows of eight, and it stands beside the tray two counters short of the heap the tray began with. The two in the dish are then carried up and added, and the rebuilt heap matches the tray counter for counter. Both rebuilt heaps stay drawn.

phases.screen: a deal stopped early, with as many counters in the leftover dish as there are plates
phases.soWhat: The remainder is always smaller than the divisor, and divisor times quotient, add the remainder, gives back the dividend.

phases.win: three deals settle, and with no plates the deal never starts and the stage says there is nowhere to put a share
phases.does: deals onto one plate, then onto as many plates as counters, then empties the tray, then tries no plates
phases.goal: dividing by one leaves a number alone, a number other than zero divided by itself is one, and dividing by zero is not possible
phases.says: Try one plate. Now as many plates as counters. Now no plates at all.
phases.check: Fill these in: twenty-seven divided by one, and twenty-seven divided by twenty-seven. Then zero divided by twenty-seven, and twenty-seven divided by zero. Which one has no answer?
phases.feels: no plates is not a small number of plates, it is nowhere at all to put a share
phases.hands: Put twelve counters onto one plate, then share them onto twelve plates. Empty the tray and deal nothing onto four plates. Then take every plate away and ask the class to deal the twelve. Let them try, and ask where the first counter should go.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many plates has the dial set? Second rung, the phase's: where would the first counter go? Third rung: the bench is cut to a heap of three, dealt onto one plate, then three plates, then none, one after the other. The pad with its not possible key stays open.

wrong.why: zero divided by a number other than zero is zero, and the two sentences use the same two words the other way round.
wrong.move: says thirty-four divided by zero is zero, because with no plates nothing seems to be handed out.
wrong.screen: the dial is turned to none and the deal control stays unlit, the thirty-four counters staying in the tray exactly as they were. The caption says there is nowhere to put a share, no number is drawn anywhere on the stage for it, and the child's zero stays in the slot beside the pad's key reading not possible.

wrong.why: the rule was heard with the word always, and it gives one only when the number is other than zero; zero shared by zero looks exactly like a number shared by itself.
wrong.move: answers one for zero divided by zero, which has no answer, by reading it as a number divided by itself.
wrong.screen: the tray is emptied and the dial turned to none together, and the deal control stays unlit exactly as it did for thirty-four, because there are no plates and so nowhere to put a share, whatever the tray holds. The caption says this one is not possible too, the rule for a number and itself is lit with the words other than zero, and the child's one stays in the slot.

phases.screen: the same heap in the tray with the rule bay open beside the plate dial
phases.soWhat: Dividing by one leaves a number alone, a number other than zero divided by itself is one, and dividing by zero is not possible.
phases.concept: Dividing by one, by itself and by zero

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment one more round is dealt from a dish that holds as many counters as there are plates. Every plate lights at once, one counter leaps from the dish to each plate in the same instant, and the dish is left holding fewer than the plates, so its lid swings shut by itself. The check bar then runs without being asked: the plates' shares stack into rows of ten beside the tray, the dish tips its last few in after them, and the rebuilt heap stands level with the tray, counter for counter. The round can be undone and dealt again as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the counters are laid out in equal rows under the fact card, the card reading the multiplication, and the two division lines under it stand blank. On the second a heap sits in the tray with the plates already set out by the dial, the leftover dish empty beside them and the four name tags lying at the side. On the third a deal stands stopped early, every plate holding the same, with as many counters in the dish as there are plates and the dish lid drawn open. On the fourth the same heap waits in the tray with the rule bay open beside the plate dial and the dial resting on one. The running count at the top left holds the rounds dealt against the counters in the heap, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the fact card, or the heap, or the open dish, or the dial, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks which number is being shared. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any heap up to ninety-nine counters and any number of plates, with the fact card, the name tags, the check bar and the rule bay all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on reading two division facts out of one multiplication, naming the four numbers, keeping the remainder below the divisor, and the rules for one, the number itself and zero.
voiceLines: A heap in the tray and a row of empty plates. Which number is being shared?
Read the rows one way. Now turn the card. What does each way divide by?
Deal one to every plate each round. Which number is being shared?
Look at the dish. Could every plate still take one more?
Try one plate. Now as many plates as counters. Now no plates at all.
A new heap. Count the plates before the first round is dealt.
Free play. Any heap, any plates, with the fact card, the tags and the rule bay open.
Deal one more round in your head. Could every plate still take one?
Every heap shared, every leftover smaller than the plates, and every heap rebuilt.

observations.why: Equal rows can be read as rows of so many or as so many rows, and each reading divides by one of the two numbers that were multiplied.
observations.soWhat: Every multiplication fact with no zero in it hands over two division facts, and both of them should be written.
observations.observe: The fact card turned round and gave a second division without a single counter moving.

observations.why: The dividend is the heap, the divisor is how many plates, the quotient is one plate's share and the remainder is what sits in the dish.
observations.soWhat: The four names belong to four different things, so each one can be pointed at before it is written.
observations.observe: Every name tag settled on only one thing on the bench.

observations.why: That many counters could give every plate one more, so the sharing was not finished yet.
observations.soWhat: The remainder is always smaller than the divisor, and a bigger one means another round is due.
observations.observe: The dish would not close while it held as many counters as there were plates.

observations.why: Sharing needs somewhere to put each share, and with no plates there is nowhere at all.
observations.soWhat: Dividing by zero is not possible for any number, so zero divided by zero is not possible either.
observations.observe: With no plates the deal never started, and no number appeared anywhere on the stage.

phases.win: both division facts settle under the fact card, one for each number that was multiplied
phases.traceback: The card turns on its own: the rows light one at a time while their count climbs, and both division facts fill in.

phases.win: one more round leaves fewer in the dish than there are plates, and the check bar rebuilds the heap exactly

Multiply back, then add what is left over. Does it make 71?

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The card turns on its own: the rows light one at a time while their count climbs, and both division facts fill in.
Phase 2: The heap is dealt a round at a time; the heap, the plates, one plate and the dish light in turn, and each number settles over its name.
Phase 3: Every plate lights with a dish counter to match, one more round is dealt from the dish, the lid closes, and the check bar rebuilds the heap.
Phase 4: Each case is dealt again; with no plates the deal never starts, the stage says there is nowhere to put a share, and no number appears.

voice.opening: Counters in equal rows, on a card that turns round.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs
voice.onFinish: Every heap shared, every leftover smaller than the plates, and every heap rebuilt.
voice.rules: Spoken on opening, as each phase begins, on each question, on a miss and on the summary page. Every line is printed in the bubble, numbers as words, by the device's own voice (Indian English first). Muting keeps the child's place; unmuting speaks on from the word it reached. If the browser refuses speech until a tap, the first line waits behind a Tap to start cover.

guide.playsOn: none: an Udgam tool opens straight on its phase; the phase's teach lines are spoken first, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

toolQuestions.source: props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions is read; the authored rows below keep their stage (fitHost returns null).

items.planQuestion: 9 times 13 is 117. Write the two division facts this one multiplication gives.

question.en: 9 times 13 is 117. Write the two division facts this one multiplication gives.

items.planAnswer: 117 divided by 13 is 9, and 117 divided by 9 is 13

items.planQuestion: 6 times 17 is 102. Write both division facts it gives.

question.en: 6 times 17 is 102. Write both division facts it gives.

items.planAnswer: 102 divided by 17 is 6, and 102 divided by 6 is 17

items.planQuestion: Take 12 away from 84 again and again until nothing is left. How many times did you take it away, and what division does that show?

question.en: Take 12 away from 84 again and again until nothing is left. How many times did you take it away, and what division does that show?

items.planAnswer: 7 times, which shows that 84 divided by 12 is 7

items.planQuestion: 79 marbles are shared equally among 6 bags. Name the dividend, the divisor, the quotient and the remainder.

question.en: 79 marbles are shared equally among 6 bags. Name the dividend, the divisor, the quotient and the remainder.

items.planAnswer: The dividend is 79, the divisor is 6, the quotient is 13 and the remainder is 1

items.planQuestion: In 95 divided by 8, which number is the dividend and which is the divisor?

question.en: In 95 divided by 8, which number is the dividend and which is the divisor?

items.planAnswer: 95 is the dividend and 8 is the divisor

items.planQuestion: 65 seeds are planted equally in 4 pots. Find the quotient and the remainder, and say what each one means.

question.en: 65 seeds are planted equally in 4 pots. Find the quotient and the remainder, and say what each one means.

items.planAnswer: The quotient is 16, the seeds in each pot, and the remainder is 1, the seed left over

items.planQuestion: A child shares 58 stickers among 7 friends, gives 7 each, and says 9 are left over. What went wrong, and what is the right answer?

question.en: A child shares 58 stickers among 7 friends, gives 7 each, and says 9 are left over. What is the mistake, and what is the right answer?

items.planAnswer: 9 left over is too many, because 7 of them could give every friend one more. The answer is 8 each, with 2 left over

items.planQuestion: Find the quotient and remainder of 71 divided by 9, and check the answer by multiplying back.

question.en: Find the quotient and remainder of 71 divided by 9, and check the answer by multiplying back.

items.planAnswer: 7 remainder 8, and 9 times 7 is 63, add 8 makes 71

items.planQuestion: A child divides a number by 5 and says the remainder is 6. How do you know straight away that this is wrong?

question.en: A child divides a number by 5 and says the remainder is 6. How do you know straight away that this cannot be right?

items.planAnswer: The remainder must be smaller than the divisor, and 6 is not smaller than 5, so one more 5 could still be shared out

items.planQuestion: Work out 34 divided by 1, 34 divided by 34, and 0 divided by 34. Then say what 34 divided by 0 is.

question.en: Work out 34 divided by 1, 34 divided by 34, and 0 divided by 34. Then say what 34 divided by 0 is.

items.planAnswer: 34 divided by 1 is 34, 34 divided by 34 is 1, 0 divided by 34 is 0, and 34 divided by 0 is not possible

items.planQuestion: Fill in the blanks: 527 divided by 1 is ___, 527 divided by 527 is ___, 0 divided by 527 is ___, and 527 divided by 0 is ___.

question.en: Fill in the blanks for 527. Divide it by 1, then by itself, and divide 0 by it.

items.planAnswer: 527, then 1, then 0, and the last is not possible

items.planQuestion: Is zero divided by zero equal to one, to zero, or not possible? Say which rule decides it.

question.en: Is zero divided by zero equal to one, to zero, or not possible? Say which rule decides it.

items.planAnswer: Not possible. Dividing by zero is not possible for any number, zero included. The rules that give one and zero hold only when the divisor is other than zero

voiceLines.en: A heap in the tray and a row of empty plates. Which number is being shared?
Read the rows one way. Now turn the card. What does each way divide by?
Deal one to every plate each round. Which number is being shared?
Look at the dish. Could every plate still take one more?
Try one plate. Now as many plates as counters. Now no plates at all.
A new heap. Count the plates before the first round is dealt.
Free play. Any heap, any plates, with the fact card, the tags and the rule bay open.
Deal one more round in your head. Could every plate still take one?
Every heap shared, every leftover smaller than the plates, and every heap rebuilt.
